quiz.prompt: Your friend is fractal wood-burning with a salvaged microwave transformer, suddenly freezes, and cannot let go of the probe. First move?

options.label: Grab them by the dry cotton hoodie and yank them backward

options.label: Kick the workbench away with your sneaker
options.feedback: High voltage arcs across damp garage floors and thin rubber soles. Stepping closer before killing power is how double fatalities happen.

options.label: Cut the main breaker or wall power first—then call 911, start CPR, and get an AED
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Never touch the victim or bench until power is confirmed dead at the source.

options.label: Turn on cabin A/C recirculation so it stays cool and sublimates slower
options.feedback: Recirculation does not bring in outside air. Do not transport dry ice in the occupied cabin.

quiz.prompt: Your dog may have chewed on a yard sago palm (cycad) and starts vomiting—yet an initial belly X-ray is clean, ammonia is normal, and liver enzyme ALT is barely over the line. What's the verified move?

options.feedback: Delaying departure to count yard seeds burns critical minutes, and DIY vomiting or charcoal—especially in a wobbly or mentally altered dog—risks aspiration while cycad neuro-vascular toxicity advances.

options.label: Call a vet or pet poison line at first suspected contact, skip home vomiting and charcoal, share clean facts, and keep rechecks.

options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Lemierre's syndrome hides behind 98% oxygen and a normal white count while a septic jugular clot seeds the lungs—and leaving the neck untouched avoids launching fresh emboli.

options.label: Massage the tender neck swelling to ease the stiffness, take borrowed antibiotics, and relax because clear lungs and a normal white count rule out sepsis.
options.feedback: Pressing or massaging a septic internal jugular clot can break infected fragments loose straight toward the lungs, while borrowed pills and reassuring early numbers delay anaerobic sepsis care.

options.label: Ride out the usual seven-day viral clock—and if an ER draws blood cultures before discharge, assume 'no news is good news' unless fever spikes.
options.feedback: Blood cultures take days to grow Fusobacterium necrophorum; leaving without knowing who owns pending results—and which symptoms demand immediate return—lets a throat infection seed the bloodstream.

quiz.prompt: Inside a well-heated living room, an older relative with Parkinson's suddenly turns drowsy, confused, slurred, and rigid—while a fingertip oximeter reads a cozy 97%. What should you do?

options.label: Chalk it up to a familiar Parkinson's flare in a warm house, adjust their home dose, and let them nap.
options.feedback: A running furnace and 97% SpO₂ cannot rule out 31.6°C (88.9°F) core hypothermia—cold-locked hemoglobin clings greedily to oxygen instead of releasing it to tissues, and DIY med tweaks stall emergency care.

options.label: Call 911 without waiting for a thermometer, cover gently with dry blankets out of drafts, and give nothing by mouth.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Sudden confusion, slurred speech, or rigidity requires emergency assessment even in a heated house, and passive dry insulation protects a hypothermic heart until monitored EMS arrives.

options.label: Run a hot bath, vigorously rub their cold arms and legs to warm them fast, and offer warm sips.
